lead: Avoiding ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is a whole-food eating approach in which people build meals from minimally processed ingredients such as fresh produce, eggs, meat, legumes and grains. In looks-focused circles it is used as a way to stay lean so that jawline and facial structure show, to cut the bloat and puffiness people associate with packaged food, and to eat for skin and steady energy for training. [1][2]

The approach rests on the NOVA classification, proposed in 2009 by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of Sao Paulo, which groups foods by the extent and purpose of processing rather than by nutrients. [1][2] Group 4, the ultra-processed foods, are industrial formulations with many ingredients, often including additives and substances rarely used in home cooking, such as flavourings, emulsifiers and hydrogenated oils. [2] Examples include most industrially made bread, frozen pizza, instant noodles, flavoured yoghurt and most junk food. [1]

Observational studies associate higher UPF intake with obesity, cardiometabolic disease and earlier death, and several South American countries advise avoiding UPFs in their dietary guidelines. [1] Critics, including Arne Astrup, describe the category as loosely defined and note that the evidence is largely observational. [1] The idea reached a general audience through books such as Chris van Tulleken's Ultra-Processed People (2023). [4]

paras: NOVA has four groups. Group 1 is unprocessed or minimally processed food such as fresh or frozen produce, grains, legumes, meat, eggs and milk. Group 2 is processed culinary ingredients such as oils, salt, sugar and butter. Group 3 is processed foods such as cheese, canned vegetables and simple breads. Group 4 is ultra-processed food.[2]

NOVA considers ingredients, processing and marketing, not nutrient content, and no universally accepted definition of UPF exists yet, including at Codex Alimentarius and EFSA.[1] The name comes from a 2010 article title and is not an acronym.[2] Monteiro's work grew out of observations in Brazil in the mid-1990s that obesity was rising among poorer households as processed products spread.[2]

Researchers at the University of Sao Paulo proposed NOVA in 2009; the name comes from a 2010 article titled 'A new classification of foods based on the extent and purpose of their processing', and Jean-Claude Moubarac of the Universite de Montreal is credited with the name, which is not an acronym. [2] The classification grew from Monteiro's research on Brazil's shift toward obesity in disadvantaged populations. [2]

The four groups run from unprocessed or minimally processed foods such as fresh fruit, grains, eggs and plain yoghurt; through processed culinary ingredients such as olive oil, salt, sugar and butter; to processed foods such as cheese, canned vegetables, salted nuts and bread; to ultra-processed foods, which include industrial products with ingredients of little or no culinary use such as high-fructose corn syrup and hydrogenated oils. [2] Brazil's Ministry of Health issued dietary guidelines in 2014, coordinated by Monteiro, whose core rule is to prefer natural or minimally processed foods and freshly made meals to ultra-processed foods; the Pan American Health Organization has adopted NOVA, and the FAO described the Brazilian guide as the first national guidelines to stress the social and economic aspects of sustainability. [2]

Wikipedia notes that UPFs became ubiquitous from the 1980s and that UPF sales have risen or stayed high in most countries since the 1990s, with 2023 figures of 58 percent of daily calories in the US and 57 percent in the UK, against 25 to 35 percent in most countries. [1]

Proponents link UPF avoidance to body composition: Wikipedia notes UPFs tend to be low in fibre and protein, high in energy density and high-glycaemic, features proposed to encourage overeating.[1] Someone aiming for a lean look may therefore swap them for whole foods. Wikipedia does not discuss skin or facial appearance in connection with UPFs. The look people describe is a leaner midsection and face from lower overall energy intake, plus less of the bloating associated with salty, soft, packaged foods. [1]

Wikipedia lists several proposed explanations for why UPFs might affect weight: low fibre and protein, high energy density, softness that allows fast eating, hyperpalatable combinations of salt, sugar and fat, high glycaemic index, and a suggested link to food addiction. [1] Others have proposed roles for additives, contaminants and high-heat processing. [1] The 2024 BMJ umbrella review noted no clear mechanism and heterogeneity between subgroups. [1]

In practice, people reading ingredient lists look for items such as emulsifiers, flavourings, sweeteners and hydrogenated oils as markers of NOVA group 4, and replace packaged breakfast cereal, flavoured yoghurt, instant noodles and ready meals with home-cooked versions. [1][2] Whole-food framings are common in fitness and physique communities, where reduced snacking and higher protein intake are used to hold a lean physique and to make weight cuts easier. [1]

Chris van Tulleken's Ultra-Processed People, published 27 April 2023, became a Sunday Times bestseller and brought the vocabulary of NOVA group 4 to a wide audience. [4] Wikipedia's page on him notes his wider work on diet as a cause of disease. [4]

Brazil, Uruguay, Peru and Ecuador have national guidelines advising people to avoid UPFs; Chile requires warning labels on some UPFs and taxes sugar-sweetened beverages; and a 2020 World Bank obesity report lists UPFs as a potential contributor. [1] The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition reviewed the evidence in 2022 and 2023 and recommended further research. [1] A 2025 national survey found over 64 percent of respondents supported UPF-related policies such as advertising limits and dye bans, and a 2026 Milbank Quarterly study compared UPFs to cigarettes and called for tobacco-style regulation, though Wikipedia notes there is no scientific consensus. [1]

A 2022 debate between Monteiro and Arne Astrup reached partial agreement that processing matters for diet quality, that most processing is harmless or beneficial and that more research is needed. [1] Critics also warn that demonising UPFs could undermine trust in science and that some UPFs support nutrition for lower-income people; the NOVA page notes it is criticised as binary and as not accounting for nutrition or fortification. [1][2]

Epidemiological studies associate UPF consumption with obesity and noncommunicable disease. A 2023 meta-analysis of 415,554 participants reported 12 percent higher type 2 diabetes risk per 10 percent increase in intake, a 2024 meta-analysis found 17 percent higher cardiovascular risk for the highest versus lowest consumers, and a 2025 meta-analysis found 15 percent higher all-cause mortality.[1] A 2024 BMJ umbrella review of 32 meta-analyses linked UPFs to adverse outcomes with possible heterogeneity between subgroups.[1]

Critics say the concept is poorly defined, that the evidence is observational, and that some processing is beneficial; a 2023 Lancet study found cereals and bread inversely associated with disease while animal-based products and sweetened drinks were most strongly associated.[1] The one frequently cited randomised trial did not control for macronutrient profile or energy density, and randomised trials have not confirmed the obesity link.[1] The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition recommended more research rather than adopting a position.[1]
A 2022 study in Australia found that avoiding UPFs could alter nutrient intakes, since many fortified breads and cereals are classed as UPF yet are recommended core foods in national guidelines.[3]

A 2023 review associated each 10 percent increase in UPF intake with higher risk of colorectal, breast and pancreatic cancers, although Wikipedia notes causation is not established. [1] A 2023 Lancet study found bread and cereals inversely associated with disease (hazard ratio 0.97) while animal-based products and artificially and sugar-sweetened beverages were associated with higher risk (1.09 each). [1] Wikipedia adds that food systems account for 26 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions and that the category raises environmental and packaging questions. [1]
No studies found testing UPF avoidance specifically for appearance outcomes such as skin or facial leanness. Observational and meta-analytic research on health outcomes is summarised above.[1][3]

lore.intro: Whole-food eating is promoted in fitness and wellness circles as a route to a leaner look, and the UPF label has become a popular shorthand through bestselling books and public-health campaigns. [1][4]

claims.claim: Ultra-processed foods drive overeating and fat gain
claims.believers: Proponents say UPFs are soft, energy-dense, hyperpalatable and eaten quickly, which encourages overeating. [1]
claims.experts: Observational studies link UPFs to obesity, but Wikipedia notes that randomised trials have not confirmed the obesity link and that the frequently cited trial did not control macronutrients or energy density. [1]

claims.claim: UPFs are as harmful as cigarettes
claims.believers: A 2026 Milbank Quarterly study compared UPFs to cigarettes and called for tobacco-style regulation. [1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes there is no scientific consensus, and critics say the category is loosely defined and mostly studied observationally. [1]

claims.claim: All processing is bad; whole foods are always better
claims.believers: The Brazilian guide advises preferring natural or minimally processed foods and freshly made meals. [2]
claims.experts: The 2022 Monteiro-Astrup debate reached agreement that most processing is harmless or beneficial; a 2023 Lancet study found cereals and bread inversely associated with disease. [1]

claims.claim: Avoiding UPFs improves skin and facial appearance
claims.believers: Wellness communities connect whole-food diets with clearer skin and a leaner face. [1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia does not discuss skin or facial appearance in relation to UPFs, and no study has tested UPF avoidance for appearance outcomes. [1]

claims.believers: Advocates describe whole-food eating as simple and low-risk. [2]
claims.experts: A 2022 Australian study found avoiding UPFs could alter nutrient intakes because many fortified breads and cereals are classed as UPFs yet recommended in national guidelines. [3]

claims.claim: UPFs are linked to higher mortality and chronic disease
claims.believers: Advocates cite meta-analyses showing 12 percent higher type 2 diabetes risk per 10 percent increase in intake and 15 percent higher all-cause mortality for the highest consumers. [1]
claims.experts: A 2024 BMJ umbrella review of 32 meta-analyses noted heterogeneity between subgroups and no clear mechanism, and the evidence is largely observational. [1]

name: Avoiding ultra-processed foods

card.summary: A whole-food approach built on the NOVA scheme; linked to health outcomes in observational studies but no appearance trials.
card.note: The UPF category is contested by some nutrition researchers.

quick.overview:
This approach means cutting industrially manufactured, multi-ingredient foods and eating mostly whole or minimally processed ones, often to reduce body fat.

Observational studies link UPFs to obesity and disease, but the category itself is debated.
quick.mechanism: NOVA classifies foods by processing rather than nutrients. Mechanisms linking UPFs to harm are described as unclear.
quick.risks: Little direct risk reported. One study noted that avoiding UPFs could change nutrient intake, since fortified breads and cereals are often classed as UPFs.
